content:
A Launch Team can talk about the neighborhood for months and never show up in it. You can also show up once, take a photo, and leave a partner short the next month. Neither one builds trust.

Join useful work a local partner already runs, and come back on a schedule you can keep. An invitation to church, and a conversation about Jesus, stay honest next steps. They are not the price of the help. This guide is not a plan for hosting your own event. Personal invitations still belong before Launch Sunday, and they are a different job from a service shift.

---

## What this pattern is

You join work someone else already coordinates. That might be a food pantry, a school supply drive, a park cleanup, or a shelter meal. Ask where help is needed, and whether a small team can take a shift the partner already posts.

Do not start a program so the church can be the host. Do not treat the shift as a quiet ad for Launch Sunday. If you want to invite someone to a gathering, say what it is and invite them as a person. The [promotion plan](/wiki/pre-launch/the-promotion-plan) and [invitation strategies](/wiki/core-group/vision-meetings/invitation-strategies) cover that. Keep invitations off the serving line unless the partner has agreed volunteers may offer them.

**Useful service.** This is the task the partner assigned. It is not a hidden church pitch.

**A church invitation.** This is an optional next step to a gathering. It is not a condition for receiving help.

**A gospel conversation.** This is a talk about Jesus when someone welcomes it. It is not a required close for every shift.

<Callout type="insight">
  Help that depends on a response is a different choice, and it is not this one. Serve because the need is real. Invite only when the person can say no and still receive the same help.
</Callout>

---

## Say the purpose out loud

Tell the Launch Team why you are going before the first shift. You are there to do the partner's work, not to collect attendance, professions of faith, or stories that make the plant look busy.

Tell the partner who you are. You are part of a church that is forming, and you want to help with work they already do. Hiding the church, then making an ask at the end, makes the next church harder to believe.

Follow their rules about what volunteers may say on site. A food line, a classroom, and a shelter desk are not your stage. If someone asks why you came, answer plainly. If they ask about Jesus or about a gathering, answer. If they do not, finish the task.

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"So then, while we have opportunity, let us do good to all people, and especially to those who are of the household of the faith."* — Galatians 6:10 (LSB)
</Callout>

Doing good is the assignment here. It does not replace Witness. The [Worship/Walk/Work/Witness model](/wiki/discovery/the-worship-walk-work-witness-model) still calls you to share Jesus in loving, intentional ways, and it warns against treating people as projects. A pantry shift is service beside neighbors. Witness is separate. Pray for people by name. Talk about Jesus where a conversation is welcome. Do not count the shift as the talk you never had.

---

## Find work that already exists

Ask who on the team already serves somewhere, and whether that group can take two or three more people on a repeating shift. A coordinator who knows one of you is easier to keep than a cold form.

See what help already exists before you invent a program. Call 211, or search by location at 211.org. 211 connects you to local help, and every call is confidential. Use it to find organizations that already serve your area, then open their volunteer pages. Do not call 211 to register the team. Do not treat people who need help as a contact list.

Read the page you are on. The National Park Service says you can volunteer for a day or year-round, on your own or with friends and family. That is an example of published terms, not a required site. Feeding America says most food banks list open shifts on their website. One food bank has you check the shift time, details, location, and open spots, requires a waiver when you register online, and starts with a brief orientation. Another requires every volunteer to register in advance, once a year or on a regular basis. Your partner may differ. Their page wins.

Before you say yes:

- [ ] A named person coordinates volunteers
- [ ] The page lists a real shift
- [ ] The work helps people outside the Launch Team
- [ ] You can name the church without hiding it
- [ ] You can meet the age rule, waiver, and any screen they name
- [ ] The shift does not collide with a gathering you already promised

If they ask for a background check, use their process. A church form does not replace it. For church roles, follow the [volunteer background check process](/wiki/launch-team/volunteer-background-check-process), and still do what the partner requires.

---

## Promise only what you can repeat

Three yeses in one meeting become three cancellations when training and setup land on the same week.

Start with one partner and one recurring slot. Put the dates on the Launch Team calendar. Name one person to own the coordinator relationship. That person confirms the roster a few days ahead and writes if someone drops. If you cannot staff the next date, say so before you promise it.

<Callout type="warning">
  Do not promise a monthly crew you do not have. One kept shift is worth more than three plans you cancel.
</Callout>

Add a second partner only after the first slot has happened more than once without a scramble. If a shift conflicts with a required gathering, say so before you register.

---

## Do the assigned work

Arrive when they asked, in what they asked you to wear. Take their coordinator's direction. Learn names. Do the dull part too.

Do not hand out church cards unless they agreed. Do not turn a line into an announcement. Do not start a faith conversation in a place they reserved for another task, such as a child's classroom or a crisis desk.

If someone asks about the church, answer, and stop when they are done. If they want to hear more, offer one next step and name it. A conversation, a Vision Meeting, or later Launch Sunday. Let them decline. The help stays the same.

---

## Keep the next step voluntary

Follow up only when someone welcomes contact. Ask how they want to be reached, and use that way once. A no, or silence, ends it. Do not add a name because someone stood near the team.

Write what the person told you. Do not record a profession of faith they did not make. A shift, a kind talk, and a later visit are different facts. Transfer from another church is not the same as a new faith. Do not score either one. A full service calendar does not show that a healthy church is forming.

If you record how you met, record the source they gave you. Do not infer a conversion. Everyfield does not judge calling, character, or spiritual health, and it does not certify the team. It will not hold the plant for a missing outreach quota. Shifts worked are not a gate.

<Callout type="important">
  Service does not fulfill Witness. Keep praying, and keep personal invitations alive. Do not make the partner's clients a project list, and do not skip Witness because the shift felt like enough.
</Callout>

---

## After you leave

Thank the coordinator. Set the next date, or say when you will confirm the roster. Debrief the same week. What did they need, who can return, and what will you refuse to count? Note an injury, a conflict, or a request you cannot meet. If the fit is gone, finish the shifts you promised, then end it in writing. Disappearing is worse than a clear no.

---

## Common mistakes

- Starting your own event because their schedule is inconvenient
- Hiding the church, then making the ask at the end
- Measuring the month by later attendance
- Bringing students without checking the age rule
- Swapping a church screening form for theirs
- Scoring professions of faith, or the lack of them
- Letting service crowd out prayer, training, and invitations

<Callout type="tip">
  Keep a one-page note. Partner, coordinator, shift time, what you may and may not say on site, and the next date you have actually promised.
</Callout>

Show up for work the neighborhood already counts on. Come back when you said you would. Let any invitation stand on its own.

claim_check.notes: Owner review by Sebastian; no model review per his 2026-10-26 instruction.

rulings: Bryan ruled B5 = Option A: "Serve with existing partners" (2026-10-26 1:31 PM ET).

Wording: title is Serving with Existing Partners, not the backlog title Outreach Events and Serving the Community, because the ruled option is partner service rather than hosted events. Slug stays pre-launch/outreach-events-and-serving-the-community so the draft path matches the brief.
Wording: the article does not teach a hosted invitation event. The brief says write only to the ruled option.

Wording: no shift quota and no required gospel presentation. How evangelistic an event is remains a methodology choice, and the ruling keeps invitations and faith conversations voluntary rather than conditions for help.
Wording: sort_order is 21, one above the highest pre-launch sort_order in seed.json, which is 20.
Wording: the reader is the Launch Team because this article is phase 4. The same commitment test applies if a Core Group starts earlier.

Wording: 211, the National Park Service, and Feeding America are named as examples of how to read an existing page, not as required partners. Houston Food Bank and Second Harvest of Silicon Valley supply the waiver, orientation, and registration examples and are not recommended over a local partner.
Consistency: honored C26 and C20 without citing those numbers in the body. Transfer growth is not a profession of faith, conversion counts are not a score, and service activity is not church health.
